title: Edward Kang develops AI to detect autism and ADHD from retina #RetinaMind #autismAI #healthtech
description: Edward Kang developed an AI called Retina Mind that claims to detect autism and ADHD from a single photo of the retina with 89% accuracy. By leveraging the biological fact that the retina and brain develop from the same tissue, the AI identifies markers linked to these neurological conditions, offering a potentially faster alternative to traditional behavioral evaluations. Although still a prototype and not yet medically approved, Retina Mind represents an innovative use of AI in neurodevelopmental diagnostics. This approach highlights the convergence of AI and biomedical science, showcasing how non-invasive imaging could transform early detection methods for autism and ADHD. The technology underscores a promising shift towards accessible, technology-driven healthcare solutions. Retina Mind raises important considerations for the future of diagnostic AI tools, emphasizing the potential to streamline and enhance patient care while prompting further validation and ethical scrutiny. #RetinaMind #EdwardKang #AutismDetection #ADHDDiagnosis #NeurodevelopmentAI #MedicalAI #AIInnovation #Biotech #HealthcareTech #AIinMedicine #EarlyDiagnosis #Neuroscience #AIPrototype #MentalHealthTech #DiagnosticAI

top_comments.author: @entityself3104
top_comments.text:
This is impressive work for a 17-year-old, but the video leaves out most of the important context.

He did not independently discover the relationship between the retina and the brain, nor did he personally collect confidential medical data. He built on existing published research, used an already prepared medical-image dataset, and had access to a specialist science school, laboratory facilities, and research mentorship.

That is still a real achievement. But “a teenager built an AI that can detect autism from a photo of your eye” is a much more dramatic story than “a student trained an experimental model on an existing labelled dataset.”

Also, 89% accuracy on a research dataset does not mean it can diagnose people in the real world. Without independent clinical validation, it may be detecting differences in cameras, hospitals, ages, or datasets rather than autism or ADHD themselves.
